Four worldsFour worlds, four kinds of concurrency

    
HPC
one huge job

      
      
Problem: split the work
Tools: OpenMP, MPI
Example: weather, Mandelbrot

    
Data center
millions of small requests

      
      
Problem: wait cheaply
Tools: coroutines, goroutines
Example: search, chat, shops

    
Web
one thread, many events

      
      
Problem: safe for every coder
Tools: event loop, async/await
Example: every web page

    
AI
one operation, huge arrays

      
      
Problem: more work per watt
Tools: SIMD, GPUs (CUDA)
Example: training, inference

    
Same threads underneath; each world picks the model that fits its work

    
Four parts and their focus from the course's earlier Lecture 20 (Xin Liu) · models from the source lecture series (parallel algorithms, asynchronous programming, CPU, GPU and SIMT)

HPCHPC cuts twice: machines, then threads

    
    
A simulation: the world as a grid of cells; each time step updates every cell from its neighbors

    
1. Machines: MPIone process per machine, separate memories, send messages

    
2. Threads: OpenMPinside a machine, threads share one memory

    
3. Talk only at the bordereach step, neighbors swap their edge cells

    
Cut the work so that the pieces talk as little as possible

    
Two levels of decomposition (machine, thread) and MPI / OpenMP from the course's earlier Lecture 20 (Xin Liu) · "scale up, scale out" from the source lecture (parallel algorithms and data structures)

  

  

    

    
HPCz ← z² + c, one pixel at a time

    

      
double mandelbrot(double x, double y) {

      
    int n = 0;

      
    double a = 0, b = 0, c, d;   // z = a + bi

      
    while ((c = a * a) + (d = b * b) < 4 && n++ < 880) {

      
        b = 2 * a * b + y * 1024 / H * 8e-9 - 0.645411;

      
        a = c - d + x * 1024 / W * 8e-9 + 0.356888;

      
    }

      
    return n;   // the pixel's color

      
}

    

    
z0 = 0,  zn+1 = zn2 + c,  c from the pixel (x, y)

HPCmandelbrot.c: one pragma, N strips

    

      
int worker_for(int x, int y) {

      
    return x / (W / nthread);

      
}

      
void T_worker(int tid) {

      
    for (int x = 0; x < W; x++)

      
        for (int y = 0; y < H; y++)

      
            if (worker_for(x, y) == tid - 1)

      
                pic[x][y] = mandelbrot(x, y);

      
}

      
int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {

      
    nthread = atoi(argv[1]);

      
    #pragma omp parallel num_threads(nthread)

      
    #pragma omp for schedule(static)

      
    for (int i = 0; i < nthread; i++)

      
        T_worker(i + 1);

      
    printf(...);   // total and per-thread time

      
}

HPCBack to sum++: count locally, add rarely

    

      
int sum_local[MAX_TID];   // one slot per thread

      
void *T_array(void *arg) {

      
    int tid = (int)(intptr_t)arg;

      
    for (long i = 0; i < TOTAL / T; i++) {

      
        if (++sum_local[tid] == S) {

      
            pthread_mutex_lock(&lk);

      
            sum += sum_local[tid];   // "sloppy" counter

      
            pthread_mutex_unlock(&lk);

      
            sum_local[tid] = 0;

      
        }

      
    }

      
    lock; sum += sum_local[tid]; unlock;   // the rest

      
}

    

    

    
    

    

    
Keep the hot counter private; touch the shared one rarely

HPCthread_local: one copy per thread

    

      
_Thread_local int x = 100;   // C11 spelling of thread_local

      

      
void *T_worker(void *arg) {

      
    int tid = (int)(intptr_t)arg;

      
    x++;

      
    printf("Thread %d: %p = %d\n", tid, (void *)&x, x);

      
}

      
int main() {

      
    /* create T1..T4, then join them */

      
    printf("main:     %p = %d\n", (void *)&x, x);

      
}

Data centerA million coroutines in one thread

    

      
def T_worker(name):

      
    i = 0

      
    while (i := i + 1):

      
        yield f"[{name}] i = {i}"   # pause here

      

      
threads = [T_worker(i) for i in range(1_000_000)]

      

      
while count < 10_000_000:

      
    current = random.choice(threads)

      
    res = current.send(None)   # run until yield

      
    count += 1

    

    
    

    

    
A coroutine is a function that can pause: 256 bytes, no kernel

    
generator.py from the source lecture's demo (coroutine), with timing and memory added · real run on this laptop: Python 3.11.9 (source/code/gen/gen.out)

  

  

    

    
Data centerOne coroutine sleeps, all of them sleep

    

      
async def T_blocking(name):

      
    print(name, "start")

      
    time.sleep(1)            # system call: the thread stops

      
    print(name, "end")

      

      
async def T_async(name):

      
    print(name, "start")

      
    await asyncio.sleep(1)   # give control back

      
    print(name, "end")

      

      
await asyncio.gather(*(worker(f"T{i}") for i in range(1, 4)))

    

    

    

    
A coroutine must never block; it yields while it waits

    
block.py (print lines shortened; the real ones also print the time), after the source lecture's point that one blocking coroutine stops them all · real run on this laptop: Python 3.11.9 asyncio (source/code/block/block.out)

  

  

    

    
Data centerGoroutines: write threads, run coroutines

    
you write

    

      
sleep(1);

      
read(fd, buf, size);

    

    
the compiler and runtime run

    

      
put_my_self_into_sleep(1); yield();

      
while (read_async(fd, buf, size) == -EAGAIN)

      
    yield();

    

    
    

    
Goroutines: used like threads, as light as coroutines

Data centerShare memory by communicating

    

      
func T_worker(name int, ch chan<- string, done <-chan struct{}) {

      
    i := 0

      
    for {

      
        i++

      
        select {

      
        case ch <- fmt.Sprintf("[%d] i = %d", name, i):

      
        case <-done: return

      
        }

      
    }

      
}

      
func main() {

      
    for i := range THREADS {           // 1,000,000

      
        channels[i] = make(chan string, 1)

      
        go T_worker(i, channels[i], done)

      
    }

      
    for count := 0; count < COUNT; count++ {

      
        res := <-channels[r.Intn(THREADS)]

      
        fmt.Println(res)

      
    }

      
}

    

    
    

    
A channel is the lock and the queue in one: pass data, not pointers

WebOne thread, one queue, run to completion

    

      
log('A  main script starts');

      
setTimeout(() => log('D  timer, 0 ms'), 0);

      
setTimeout(() => log('F  timer, 100 ms'), 100);

      
fs.readFile(__filename, () => log('E  file read done'));

      
Promise.resolve().then(() => log('C  promise callback'));

      
const end = Date.now() + 500;

      
while (Date.now() < end) {}   // busy for 500 ms

      
log('B  main script ends');

    

    

    

    

    
A callback never interrupts another: no data race, no lock

WebCallbacks: a straight line cut into pieces

    

      
function withCallbacks(done) {

      
  get('/api/user', user => {

      
    log('user', user);

      
    get(`/api/user/${user.id}/friends`, friends => {

      
      log('friends', friends);

      
      get(`/api/friend/${friends[0].id}`, friend => {

      
        log('friend', friend);

      
        done();

      
      });

      
    });

      
  });

      
}

    

    

    

    
Callbacks cut one straight story into nested pieces

    
The user / friends / friend chain from the source lecture ($.ajax with success callbacks), rewritten for Node · api.js: a local server answers each request after 1 s; real run on this laptop, node v26.13.1 (source/code/web/api.out)

  

  

    

    
Webasync/await: write in order, run as a graph

    

      
async function withAwait() {

      
  const user = await fetchJSON('/api/user');

      
  const friends = await fetchJSON(`/api/user/${user.id}/friends`);

      
  const friend = await fetchJSON(`/api/friend/${friends[0].id}`);

      
}

      

      
async function withAll() {   // three independent requests

      
  const [u, f, g] = await Promise.all([fetchJSON('/api/user'),

      
      fetchJSON('/api/user/7/friends'), fetchJSON('/api/friend/42')]);

      
}

    

    

    

    
await writes the order; Promise.all lets independent work overlap

    
async/await and Promise.all from the source lecture (asynchronous programming) · api.js, real run on this laptop: node v26.13.1, each request answered after 1 s (source/code/web/api.out)

AIA shader is spawn() for every pixel

    
the idea
      
void T_kernel(int row, int col) {

      
    screen[row * 1920 + col] = f(row, col);

      
}

      
for (row = 0; row < 1080; ++row)

      
    for (col = 0; col < 1920; ++col)

      
        spawn(T_kernel, row, col);   // 2,073,600 threads

    

    
mandelbrot.cu
      
__global__ void mandelbrot_kernel(int *pic_d) {

      
    int x = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;

      
    int y = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;

      
    if (x < W && y < H)

      
        pic_d[y * W + x] = mandelbrot(x, y);

      
}

      
mandelbrot_kernel<<<gridDim, blockDim>>>(pic_d);   // launch

    

    
    

    
CUDA: write the work for one pixel; the GPU runs it for all of them

AISIMT: one PC drives 32 threads

    
mandelbrot.ptx
      
mov.u32    %r5, %ctaid.x;    // blockIdx.x

      
mov.u32    %r7, %tid.x;      // threadIdx.x

      
mad.lo.s32 %r1, %r5, %r6, %r7;  // x

      
...

      
$L__BB0_2:

      
fma.rn.f64 %fd22, %fd29, %fd21, %fd1;

      
mul.f64    %fd28, %fd30, %fd30;

      
mul.f64    %fd27, %fd29, %fd29;

      
add.f64    %fd25, %fd28, %fd27;

      
setp.lt.f64 %p4, %fd25, 0d4010000000000000;  // < 4

      
...

      
@%p6 bra   $L__BB0_2;

      
...

      
mad.lo.s32 %r14, %r2, 12800, %r1;  // y * W + x

      
st.global.u32 [%rd4], %r13;
